title: Components of population dynamics
competency: Calculate birth rate, death rate and net migration rate, and explain what affects them.

keywords.def: The actual reproductive performance of a population.
Live births in a year for every 1,000 people. BR = (B ÷ P) × 1000.
The occurrence of death in a human population.
Deaths in a year for every 1,000 people. DR = (D ÷ P) × 1000.
The death of young children below one year of age.
The movement of people from one place to another.
A person leaving one country to live in another (out-migrant).
A person entering a country from another to make a new home (in-migrant).
Immigrants minus emigrants, per 1,000 people in a year.

en.text: Population changes through three components: fertility, mortality and migration. Fertility and mortality are biological; migration is not. Fertility is the actual reproductive performance of a population. Birth rate is live births per 1,000 people in a year: BR = (B ÷ P) × 1000.

screens.title: Why do numbers change?
screens.ask: What makes the size of a population change?
opts: Births, deaths and people moving in or out
screens.after: Three things: births (fertility), deaths (mortality) and migration.

screens.title: 2.2.1 Components of population dynamics
paras: The main components are fertility, mortality and migration.
Fertility and mortality are biological factors. Migration is non-biological.
Together they control changes in population size and composition.

screens.title: A. Fertility
paras: Fertility is the actual reproductive performance of a population.
World population growth depends largely on fertility.
The most common measure of fertility is the birth rate.

screens.title: Birth rate (BR)
paras: Birth rate is the number of live births in one year for every 1,000 people.
BR = (B ÷ P) × K
B = live births in the year, P = mid-year population, K = 1000.

screens.title: Work out a birth rate
steps: Activity 2.3 B1: place A had 2,400 live births and 160,000 people.
So BR = 15 births per 1,000 people per year.

screens.title: Factors of fertility
paras: Low access to contraceptives; backwardness and poverty.
Low status of women; need of children for labour.
Children seen as a symbol of virility; low educational background.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The actual reproductive performance of a population.
Live births in a year for every 1,000 people. BR = (B ÷ P) × 1000.

screens.ask: A town has 2,000 live births and 100,000 people. BR = (2,000 ÷ 100,000) × 1000 = ___ per 1,000.
screens.clue: Divide births by population, then multiply by 1000.

screens.text: Migration is a biological factor that determines the size of population.
screens.why: Fertility and mortality are biological. Migration is non-biological.

screens.text: Which factors raise fertility, according to the book? Tap all.
screens.why: The four chosen are on the book's list. Education and family planning lower fertility.

screens.ask: Region X has 450,000 people and a birth rate of 30 per 1,000. How many live births is that in a year? ___
screens.clue: Each 1,000 people have 30 births. How many thousands are there?

en.text: Mortality is the occurrence of death in a population. Death rate is deaths per 1,000 people in a year: DR = (D ÷ P) × 1000. Rate of natural increase = birth rate − death rate. Infant mortality is the death of children under one year.

screens.title: Where do more people die young?
screens.ask: In which countries do you think death rates are usually higher?
screens.after: Death rates are higher in developing countries. Living standards, food, medical care and sanitation differ.

screens.title: B. Mortality
paras: Mortality is the occurrence of death in the human population.
It is higher in developing countries than in developed ones.
The causes are differences in living standards, nutrition, medical services, hygiene and sanitation.

screens.title: Death rate (DR)
paras: DR = (D ÷ P) × K, where D = deaths, P = mid-year population, K = 1000.
Example: 21,000 deaths in a population of 7,000,000.

screens.title: Focus
paras: Rate of natural increase = birth rate − death rate.
Infant mortality is the death of children below one year.
table: High incidence of disease and infections

screens.title: Key words
defs: The occurrence of death in a human population.
Deaths in a year for every 1,000 people. DR = (D ÷ P) × 1000.
The death of young children below one year of age.

screens.ask: A district has 900 deaths and 150,000 people. DR = (900 ÷ 150,000) × 1000 = ___ per 1,000.
Birth rate 35 per 1,000, death rate 9 per 1,000. Rate of natural increase = ___ per 1,000.
screens.clue: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate.

screens.ask: Place B had 219,300 deaths and 19,297,000 people. DR = ___ per 1,000 (one decimal place).
screens.clue: Divide, then multiply by 1000. Round to one decimal place.

screens.text: Which one is a cause of high death rate?
screens.why: Famine is on the book's list of causes.

screens.ask: A town has 80,000 people. Its birth rate is 32 and death rate 7 per 1,000. By how many people does it grow naturally in one year? ___
screens.clue: Find the rate of natural increase first.

en.text: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. Push factors like poor jobs, war and harsh climate make people leave. Pull factors like good jobs, good climate and services attract them. Net migration rate = (immigrants − emigrants) ÷ population × 1000.

screens.title: Push or pull?
screens.ask: Almaz moves from a dry village to Hawassa for a job. Which reason is a "pull" factor?
screens.after: A good job attracts, or pulls, people. Drought and war push people away.

screens.title: C. Migration
paras: Migration is the movement of humans from one place to another.
Push factors put pressure on people to leave: poor employment, civil war, harsh climate.
Pull factors attract people: good job opportunity, favourable climate, good welfare service.

screens.title: Emigrants and immigrants
paras: An emigrant (out-migrant) leaves one country to live in another.
An immigrant (in-migrant) enters a country from another to make a new home.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The movement of people from one place to another.
A person leaving one country to live in another (out-migrant).
A person entering a country from another to make a new home (in-migrant).
Immigrants minus emigrants, per 1,000 people in a year.

screens.why: Push factors make people leave; pull factors attract them.
screens.clue: Does it drive people away or draw them in?

screens.ask: A person who is leaving one country to live in another is an ___.
Emigrants 30,000, immigrants 150,000, population 100 million. NMR = ___ per 1,000.

screens.text: A region has 40,000 emigrants and 10,000 immigrants in a year. What does its net migration show?
screens.why: 10,000 − 40,000 = −30,000. More people leave than arrive, so the NMR is negative: a net loss.
screens.clue: Work out immigrants − emigrants. Is it positive or negative?

items.text: A1. Why is fertility higher in developing countries?
opts: Low access to contraceptives, poverty, low status of women and low education
items.ans: Low access to contraceptives, poverty, low status of women and low education
items.why: These are the book's factors of fertility.

items.text: A2. What are major causes of high death rate? Tap all.
items.why: These are on the book's list.

items.ask: B1. Live births 2,400, mid-year population 160,000. BR = ___ per 1,000.
B2. Deaths 219,300, mid-year population 19,297,000. DR = ___ per 1,000.

notes.text: The book's birth-rate example (150,800 births in 50,686,000 people) gives 2.975, printed as 2.9; correct rounding is 3.0, and the numbers are unrealistic (real rates are 30–40 per 1,000). The example is left out of the lesson; teacher to check.
Activity 2.3 A questions are open; they are given as choices based on the book's lists.
